newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Soyuz space capsule lands, Russian crew well.
newsitem.headline: Soyuz space capsule lands, Russian crew well.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts emerged smiling from their Soyuz space capsule on Thursday shortly after it landed on the parched Kazakh steppes.

Minutes before, applause had burst out at Mission Control near Moscow. Officials keeping radio contact with the crew had been waiting in tense silence for the landing, which was apparently delayed by slightly more than one minute.

Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin looked tired but well after the gruelling trip, which followed six months on the Mir space station -- one of the toughest missions in the history of manned space flight.

The cosmonauts, obviously very thirsty, drank some water, and then doctors started extensive medical tests. Chief mission doctor Igor Goncharov said Tsibliyev's condition, including his heart and pulse rate, were satisfactory.
Tsibliyev said he felt "happy to be back on earth".

The commander had developed stress-induced heart trouble after Mir collided with a cargo craft he was manoeuvring on June 25, cutting power to the station in the worst accident in its 11-year history.
Despite his cardiac problem, he seemed to be the more lively of the two.
Two helicopters bearing rescue teams arrived at the remote desert spot where Soyuz landed after a 15-minute descent through the earth's atmosphere on a huge yellow and white parachute.

If deemed fit enough, the men were due to be transferred 170 km (100 miles) to the airport in Dzhezkazgan, the nearest sizeable town in the sparsely populated former Soviet republic. From there they were due to fly to Moscow.

The families of the two men were to greet them at the Star City cosmonaut training centre outside Moscow. They sent a package of gifts for the crew, including a bottle of Tsibliyev's favourite French red wine.
